scenes.heading: Area of composite shapes
scenes.sub: Break it into shapes you know
scenes.say: An L-shaped room, a shed wall with a door cut out, a garden bed shaped like a trapezium. How do you find their areas? Break them into shapes you already know.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Cut an L-shaped cake into two rectangles, or imagine the full tin minus a corner
scenes.science: Composite area: add the pieces, or subtract the missing part
scenes.breaks: A real cake has thickness, but area is only about the flat top surface.
scenes.say: Imagine a cake baked in an L-shaped tin. You could cut it into two rectangles and add them up. Or picture the full rectangular tin and take away the empty corner. Both ways give the same amount of cake. That's exactly how composite areas work.

scenes.heading: Trapezium
scenes.say: A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides, a and b. Its area is a half times a plus b, times the height. Two copies make a parallelogram, which is why we halve.
scenes.caption: Trapezium: A = ½ × (a + b) × h. Two copies make a parallelogram, so we halve.

scenes.heading: Two trapeziums make a parallelogram
notes: Height h is at right angles
scenes.say: Here's a trapezium. First the shape, then the two parallel sides, a on top and b on the bottom. The dashed line is the height, h. It must meet the parallel sides at right angles, not run along the sloping edge.

scenes.heading: Rhombus or kite
parts: the shape fills half its rectangle
scenes.say: For a rhombus or a kite, use the diagonals, the lines joining opposite corners. The area is a half times x times y, because the shape fills exactly half the rectangle drawn around it.
scenes.caption: Rhombus or kite: A = ½ × x × y, using the diagonals.

scenes.heading: Trapezium example
scenes.question: Parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, perpendicular height 4 cm. Find the area.
scenes.say: A trapezium has parallel sides of six and ten centimetres and a height of four. Add the parallel sides: sixteen. Half of sixteen is eight, and eight times four is thirty-two square centimetres.
scenes.caption: 6 + 10 = 16. ½ × 16 = 8, and 8 × 4 = 32 cm².

scenes.heading: Subtraction method
scenes.question: An L-shaped room fits in a 10 m by 8 m rectangle, with a 4 m by 3 m corner missing. Find its area.
scenes.say: An L-shaped room fits inside a ten by eight metre rectangle, with a four by three corner missing. The big rectangle is eighty square metres. The corner is twelve. Eighty take away twelve is sixty-eight square metres.
scenes.caption: Big rectangle 10 × 8 = 80 m². Missing corner 4 × 3 = 12 m². 80 − 12 = 68 m².

scenes.heading: Subtract the missing corner
scenes.say: Watch the L-shaped room appear. The pink corner is the missing part, four metres by three metres. Picture the full rectangle, then take the corner away.
scenes.caption: The pink corner, 4 m by 3 m, is missing. Picture the full 10 m by 8 m rectangle, then take the corner away.

scenes.heading: Two ways to do it

right.title: Subtract the gaps
points: Draw a big shape around it

scenes.say: So you have two methods. Add the bits: split the shape and add the pieces. Or subtract the gaps: start with a big shape and take away what's missing, like a door or a window. Choose whichever has simpler pieces.

points: Rhombus or kite: ½ × x × y
Add the bits or subtract the gaps
scenes.say: Quick recap. Trapezium, a half times a plus b, times h. Rhombus or kite, a half times the diagonals. For composite shapes, add the bits or subtract the gaps, and find any missing lengths first. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Trapezium: ½ × (a + b) × h. Rhombus or kite: ½ × x × y. Add the bits or subtract the gaps, and find missing lengths first. Now try the practice questions!
